comparator.name: Criminology
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted 2026–2027 regulations, Articles 7.1, 9.1, 10.2 and 11.3, establish the general Dutch-language bachelor. Years one and two each contain ten required 6 EC courses. Year three includes three 6 EC courses, the 12 EC research unit and 30 EC of open study. Principles of Criminal Law precedes substantive and procedural criminal law. The ordinary research route requires quantitative and qualitative criminological methods and combines a group investigation with an individual thesis. The current module describes a conditional enrolment process for students completing qualitative methods in the same academic year. It does not alter the ordinary progression. The Dutch language test and any required refresher are conditions for the first-year project grade without separate credits. The forensic minor is optional.
components: Aard, omvang en schade van criminaliteit
Kwantitatieve methoden en technieken van criminologisch onderzoek (academische kern)
Kwalitatieve methoden en technieken van criminologisch onderzoek

core: Crime, criminal law and responses by justice institutions
Psychological and life-course explanations of offending and victimisation
Social causes, harms and prevention of crime
Quantitative and qualitative empirical criminological research
adjacent: Media narratives about crime and the social meaning of justice
Violent conflict, social trust and public safety
questions: Why do individuals offend, and how do life-course and mental-health factors matter?
How do legal and social institutions prevent and punish crime?
What evidence can clarify crime, its harms and responses?

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Introduces legal systems, criminal and public law, legal reasoning, law-society relationships and trial simulations as foundations for examining criminal accountability.
introduces social structures and inequalities relevant to crime contexts
Studies rights treaties, monitoring and case law, liberty and equality; supplies a specific rights-based complement for evaluating state responses to offending, without teaching criminal procedure.
Develops behavioral, clinical-psychological and neural foundations for later study of social influence, mental disorder and development; does not itself explain criminal behavior.
studies social influence, norms and behavior in groups
develops qualitative interviews and interpretation of social evidence
Provides virtue, deontological and consequentialist reasoning and moral responsibility as a normative complement for evaluating criminalization and punishment.
Studies criminal liability, legality and defenses. Applies legal reasoning in a simulated legal aid clinic and develops a criminology research proposal.
develops statistical and experimental methods for behavioral evidence
Examines justifications of political power and its limits, supporting normative assessment of state authority in criminal justice rather than teaching policing institutions.
Introduces clinical assessment and psychotherapies. Students evaluate evidence and practise introductory assessment methods.
studies human development across the lifespan and related behavioral change
Includes international criminal law and law of armed conflict within a wider public-international-law survey; a bounded extension to legal accountability, not domestic criminal procedure.

Examines social trust, solidarity, the public sphere and civil repair, with a civil-society organization study; complements examination of social responses to harm without claiming dedicated crime-prevention instruction.
Examines how film, photographs and other media represent race, crime, punishment and resistance in American history.
introduces data analysis and visualisation for social evidence
Uses systematic review, effect sizes and meta-analysis in R to synthesize findings across studies.
Examines causes and dynamics of violence, conflict and peacebuilding across institutional and civil-society settings; a related violence/justice perspective, not a substitute for domestic penology.
Studies gender and inequality through primary sources and historical research. Incarceration is one topic in its wider North American history.
Develops operationalization, sampling, survey/experimental design, descriptive and inferential statistics and a group empirical project; provides the foundation for subsequent multivariate analysis.

Studies modern sociological theories and colonial contexts as explicit social-theory foundations for examining social structures and interpreting the later civil-society course; not a criminological theory sequence.
Examines how biological, psychological and social factors inform the classification, assessment and treatment of mental disorders.
Uses psychology and social science to examine youth radicalization and design evidence-based materials for schools and youth educators.

alternatives.label: Crime, psychology and justice
alternatives.concept: Studies criminal responsibility and prevention through law, psychology and sociology. Students investigate how young people become vulnerable to radicalization, how public institutions respond to harm, and how media and historical sources represent incarceration and inequality. Quantitative, qualitative and evidence-synthesis methods support that work.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed programme combines legal accountability, social and clinical psychology, sociology and empirical methods; prevention and representation make specific contributions without claiming a complete criminology qualification.
progression: Law, Society & Justice precedes Criminal Law & Criminal Justice and Public International Law. Research Methods & Statistics precedes multivariable analysis and meta-analysis. Introduction to Brain & Behavior precedes the developmental and clinical courses, with Psychopathology taken before Psychodiagnostics & Psychotherapies.

selection.assessment: One qualified response is retained. Cybercrime is a genuine target interest, but general data analysis does not establish a digital-offending/investigation programme. The forensic minor concerns forensic psychiatry, legal psychology, penology, rehabilitation and forensic linguistics. The closest response already includes the available clinical, developmental and criminal-law contributions; a second forensic label would not yield a distinct supported 24-course curriculum. No third concept is considered after the second fails.

Both examine criminal liability, defenses and legal reasoning. UCR applies the principles in a simulated legal aid clinic.
UCR studies criminal liability and rights. VU gives policing and criminal justice institutions dedicated attention.
UCR covers criminal law in a course paired with VU’s substantive criminal law unit.
UCR surveys constitutional law as part of a wider legal introduction. VU requires a dedicated public-law course.
UCR teaches data analysis and research methods. VU focuses on measuring the extent and harms of crime.
UCR studies liability, rights and international legal frameworks. VU requires a dedicated course on criminal procedure.
Both introduce psychological explanations of behaviour. UCR gives particular attention to neuroscience and mental processes.
Both examine development across the lifespan. VU focuses on criminal careers. UCR studies physical, cognitive, social and emotional development.
Both introduce sociological reasoning, theory and research. UCR applies these to inequality and social structures.
UCR studies selected aspects of crime through law, psychology and social inquiry. VU introduces criminology as a field.
UCR studies social and psychological theories that inform the study of crime. VU focuses on competing criminological explanations.
UCR examines selected forms of social harm and inequality. VU teaches victimisation in a dedicated course.
Both investigate how to prevent harm using research. UCR focuses on youth radicalization and educational responses. VU covers crime prevention and punishment more broadly.
Both develop qualitative research design, data collection and interpretation. UCR applies these methods to broader social questions.
Both use multivariable methods to analyze data. UCR covers group comparisons, categorical outcomes and latent constructs in behavioural research.
Both analyze narratives about crime and social responses. UCR studies race, crime and punishment in American media. VU teaches narrative criminology and systematic qualitative media analysis.
UCR designs empirical studies and a criminology proposal in separate courses. VU requires a first-year criminology project.
UCR develops statistical methods across introductory and advanced courses. VU requires a second dedicated statistics unit.
UCR studies moral reasoning and legal accountability in separate courses. VU applies these questions to criminological policy and responsibility.
UCR includes historical work on incarceration and inequality. VU requires dedicated historical criminology.
UCR develops empirical design, statistics and multivariable analysis across courses. VU applies these methods specifically to crime research.
VU requires group investigation and an individual criminology thesis. UCR’s optional independent research is additional to the displayed schedule.
VU reserves 30 EC for a minor or an approved package of electives.
Both introduce descriptive and inferential statistics. UCR also designs and conducts a general group study.

notes.text: VU requires dedicated study of crime measurement, criminological theory and history, criminal procedure and victimology. Its final research unit focuses on crime. UCR develops related methods and covers selected aspects of crime and punishment. Its clinical courses study general psychological assessment and treatment.

audience.programmeDescription: VU Criminology examines offending, victims, criminalization and society’s responses through criminological theory, law, psychology, sociology and empirical research. Its Dutch-language degree includes a group investigation with an individual thesis and an open minor period.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR offers one approach that combines criminal law, psychology, sociology and empirical research. Youth Resilience to Extremism provides a focused example of prevention, and media and history courses help students examine how inequality and criminal justice are represented.

curriculum.limitation: The Dutch-language degree has 60 EC of required study in each of the first two years. Year three includes 30 EC of open study and a 12 EC research unit within the required courses. The research unit normally follows both criminological methods courses and combines a group investigation with an individual thesis.

componentNotes.y3-03: The research unit follows quantitative and qualitative criminological methods.
componentNotes.y3-05: The 30 EC can include a minor or approved elective study. Forensic Criminology is one minor option.
